description: Per-translation glossary overlay for the Wheel of Heaven Translation of Thánh Ngôn Hiệp Tuyển, Quyển Nhứt (Compilation of Divine Messages, Volume One; the Caodai séance canon of 1925–26, first compiled Tòa Thánh Tây Ninh 1928). This is the pipeline's FIRST Vietnamese source text. Because the source is quốc ngữ (Latin script), there is no transliteration layer; the composition-specific decisions logged here instead concern rendering conventions (poetry, Hán-Việt register-marking, French colonial date-lines), the retain-vs-translate line for the Caodai divine-name and sacerdotal vocabulary, the four-tier Thần–Thánh–Tiên–Phật celestial hierarchy, the spirit-writing (cơ bút) apparatus, the Chơn-Thần / périsprit anthropology, the Càn-Khôn cosmology, the Đạo / -Giáo 'Way vs religion' split, the doctrinally-loaded prostration counts, the Sino-Vietnamese deity-name identifications, and the single-witness collation framework with its retained cruxes pending a printed Tòa Thánh Tây Ninh witness. Two decisions are surfaced for the human reviewer in chapter-1-editor-report.md and are NOT silently settled here: (1) the standardization of Tam Kỳ Phổ Độ to 'Third Universal Amnesty' (the established project rendering; literal sense 'universal deliverance/salvation'), which is committed as an entry but flagged for confirmation; and (2) the book-voice ruling (Thầy = third-person 'the Master' vs first-person 'I, your Master'), committed as the third-person reading with the first-person alternative flagged. NO claim_type=speculative entry is committed: the Wheel of Heaven comparative-resonance loci (the descending-teacher motif, the séance 'higher intelligence' frame, the syncretic single-identity formula of v69) are deliberately kept OUT of the surface text and the apparatus, and are escalated to the reviewer as wiki/article material rather than translation-apparatus material, per the lens-lives-in-the-apparatus rule. The English is an independent scholarly rendering and does not lift the existing English Caodai translations (daotam.info / Sydney Centre for Studies in Caodaism). Entries may be promoted to the central production glossary if the lemma acquires cross-corpus reach in subsequent Vietnamese / East-Asian-syncretic texts.

entries.lemma: the project-specific rendering conventions for the Vietnamese (quốc ngữ) source of TNHT: (1) NO transliteration field — quốc ngữ is already Latin script, so the source vi field is self-transliterating and no translit layer is generated; (2) POETRY is rendered faithful-literal, one English line per source line, preserving line count and line breaks, with NO forced English metre or rhyme, because roughly a third of the chapter is regulated Đường-luật (Tang-regulated) verse whose tonal prosody and end-rhyme cannot be reproduced without distorting sense; (3) CLASSICAL SINO-VIETNAMESE (Hán-Việt) passages that shift register out of the vernacular (vv. 54, 69, 72-73, 85, 108) are translated into English with the key romanized Hán-Việt phrase retained in brackets, marking the register shift; (4) the FRENCH colonial-era date-lines (NOEL 1925, 3 Janvier 1926, 20 Février 1926 …) are rendered with English month-names, while the Vietnamese lunar/sexagenary dates (13 tháng Giêng năm Bính-Dần) are kept transliterated and glossed '[lunar]'; (5) Unicode is NFC-normalized and the witness's legacy U+00D0 (Ð ETH) is normalized to the correct Vietnamese U+0110 (Đ)
entries.literal: the quốc-ngữ rendering conventions (no-translit; literal verse; Hán-Việt bracket-marking; French-date Englishing; NFC)
entries.standardEnglish: n/a — a project convention, not a lexical item
entries.wohChoice: the conventions as stated: no transliteration layer; line-for-line literal verse without forced metre/rhyme; Hán-Việt register-marked by bracketed romanization; French date-lines Englished, lunar dates transliterated; NFC + ETH→Đ normalization
entries.rationale: TNHT is the pipeline's first Latin-script source text, so the transliteration-convention machinery used for the Arabic (Qur'an-WoH, Hidden-Words-WoH) and Hebrew sources does not apply and its absence must be documented rather than left as an apparent omission. The poetry policy follows the same faithful-literal discipline the program uses elsewhere: the Đường-luật regulated forms (thất-ngôn bát-cú and tứ-tuyệt, e.g. vv. 3, 20, 21, 24, 29, 31, 34) depend on level/oblique tonal patterning and a fixed rhyme scheme that English cannot carry, so reproducing metre would force paraphrase and violate accuracy-before-lens; the WoH rendering therefore keeps one English line per source line and lets the commentary note the form. The Hán-Việt bracket-marking convention preserves for the reader the fact that the text code-switches into literary Classical Chinese / Sino-Vietnamese at doctrinally weighted moments, exactly as the Qur'an-WoH apparatus marks embedded registers. Named references for the conventions: the Đường-luật prosody described in Dương Quảng Hàm, Việt-Nam Văn-học Sử-yếu (1941); the quốc-ngữ orthography of Alexandre de Rhodes' Dictionarium Annamiticum (1651) as the Latin-script baseline; the Unicode NFC normalization standard (UAX #15).

entries.source: Ngọc-Hoàng Thượng-Đế Viết Cao-Đài / Tiên Ông Đại Bồ-Tát Ma-Ha-Tát / Giáo Đạo Nam Phương
entries.translit: Ngọc-Hoàng Thượng-Đế Viết Cao-Đài / Tiên Ông Đại Bồ-Tát Ma-Ha-Tát / Giáo Đạo Nam Phương
entries.lemma: the fixed three-line divine-signature header that opens eight of the ten messages (vv. 2, 7, 19, 38, 60, 68, 79, 105): 'Ngọc-Hoàng Thượng-Đế Viết Cao-Đài' (玉皇上帝曰高臺, 'the Jade Emperor, the Supreme Being, styled Cao Đài'), where Viết = Sino-Vietnamese 曰 'is called / styled / says'; 'Tiên Ông Đại Bồ-Tát Ma-Ha-Tát' (仙翁大菩薩摩訶薩, 'the Immortal Elder, Great Bodhisattva Mahāsattva'); 'Giáo Đạo Nam Phương' (教道南方, 'teaching the Way in the Southern Quarter' — i.e. to Vietnam / the South)
entries.partOfSpeech: Caodai liturgical signature-formula (compound Sino-Vietnamese divine title)
entries.literal: The Jade-Emperor Supreme-Deity, styled High-Tower / Immortal-Elder Great-Bodhisattva Mahāsattva / teaching the Way [in the] Southern Quarter
entries.standardEnglish: existing English Caodai usage often retains the whole line untranslated as a liturgical signature or transliterates it wholesale
entries.wohChoice: rendered in full and identically at each of the eight occurrences ('The Jade Emperor, the Supreme Being, styled Cao Đài, / the Immortal Elder, Great Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, / teaching the Way in the Southern Quarter.'), with Cao Đài retained as a proper name and Viết read 'styled'; per-verse commentary is written ONCE at the first occurrence (v. 2) and the remaining seven carry only a short cross-reference (render-once-comment convention), since the English line is invariant
entries.rationale: The header is a fixed liturgical formula, not free prose, and the load-bearing decisions are (a) whether to translate it at all and (b) how to parse the compound title. Because each occurrence is its own verse (refId) in a verse-keyed system that may display paragraphs independently, the header is rendered in full at every occurrence rather than translated once and cross-referenced in the surface text — a downstream consumer showing only v. 60 must still see the title — but the explanatory commentary is written once (v. 2) to avoid eight identical notes. The parse is philologically straightforward: Ngọc-Hoàng Thượng-Đế is the standard Sino-Vietnamese for the Daoist supreme sovereign (玉皇上帝, the Jade Emperor), here appositively identified with Cao Đài; Viết is 曰 'to be called/styled'; Tiên Ông 'Immortal Elder' and the Buddhist honorific Đại Bồ-Tát Ma-Ha-Tát (mahā-bodhisattva mahāsattva) are retained-and-glossed as the syncretic titles they are; Giáo Đạo Nam Phương names the mission field (the South = Vietnam). Named references: Đào Duy Anh, Hán-Việt Từ-điển, s.vv. 玉皇, 曰, 菩薩; Janet Hoskins, The Divine Eye and the Diaspora (Hawai'i, 2015), on the Cao Đài / Jade Emperor identification.

entries.source: Thầy / Ta / con / các con / Môn-đệ
entries.translit: Thầy / Ta / con / các con / Môn-đệ
entries.lemma: the book's pronominal voice: Thầy (lit. 'Master, Teacher') is God's habitual self-designation to the disciples in the vernacular teaching-prose; Ta (archaic/imperial first-person 'I') is God's self-reference in the high poetic and formal register (esp. the Ngọc-Hoàng quatrains, vv. 3, 4, 20, 31); con / các con ('child / children') is the correlative address to the disciples; Môn-đệ / đệ-tử ('disciples')
entries.partOfSpeech: Vietnamese kinship/role pronoun system (divine speaker register)
entries.literal: Thầy = Master/Teacher (first-person self-reference by role-noun); Ta = I (imperial); con/các con = child/children; Môn-đệ = disciples
entries.standardEnglish: existing English Caodai renderings vary between 'Master' (third person) and 'I' for Thầy, often inconsistently within one text
entries.wohChoice: BOOK VOICE (committed, flagged for reviewer): Thầy = 'the Master' (third-person self-designation) throughout the teaching-prose, preserving the pedagogical role-noun; Ta = 'I / Me' in the poetic-imperial register, maintaining a DELIBERATE register contrast; con / các con = 'my child / my children'; Môn-đệ / đệ-tử = 'disciples'. The first-person alternative ('I, your Master') is recorded as the reviewer-swappable option
entries.rationale: In the Vietnamese kinship-pronoun system a speaker routinely refers to himself by a role-noun rather than a bare pronoun, so Thầy ('Master/Teacher') is grammatically a first-person self-reference: 'Thầy dặn các con' denotes 'I (your Master) instruct you (my children).' The English decision is therefore stylistic, not referential, and both renderings are defensible: 'I' is more natural to direct address, but 'the Master' preserves the doctrinally central teacher-disciple framing that Caodai foregrounds in every clause and that a bare 'I' would erase, and it keeps a clean contrast with the imperial Ta of the high quatrains, which the draft already rendered 'I/Me' — a contrast the WoH translation ratifies. The choice is marked inferred (a defensible register reading, not the single consensus) and is flagged in the editor report so the reviewer may swap the whole book to first-person if readability is preferred over role-foregrounding; because the referent is unambiguous to a Vietnamese reader either way, neither reading violates accuracy-before-lens. Named references: Nguyễn Đình-Hoà, Vietnamese-English Dictionary and the kinship-pronoun analysis in his Vietnamese (London Oriental, 1997); Đào Duy Anh, Hán-Việt Từ-điển s.v. 師 (sư/thầy).

entries.source: Cao Đài / Ngọc-Hoàng Thượng-Đế / Ngọc Đế / Tiên Ông / Đức Chí Tôn / Đại-Từ-Phụ / Bạch-Ngọc-Kinh / Thiên-Đình
entries.translit: Cao Đài / Ngọc-Hoàng Thượng-Đế / Ngọc Đế / Tiên Ông / Đức Chí Tôn / Đại-Từ-Phụ / Bạch-Ngọc-Kinh / Thiên-Đình
entries.lemma: the core divine-name field: Cao Đài (高臺, lit. 'High Tower/Terrace/Palace'), the proper name of the Caodai supreme God; Ngọc-Hoàng Thượng-Đế (玉皇上帝, 'the Jade Emperor, the Supreme Being') and its short form Ngọc Đế (玉帝, 'the Jade Emperor'); Tiên Ông (仙翁, 'the Immortal Elder'); Đức Chí Tôn (至尊, 'the Most High / Supreme Being', a title implied though not lexicalized in ch. 1); Đại-Từ-Phụ (大慈父, 'the Great Merciful Father', v. 32); the celestial toponyms Bạch-Ngọc-Kinh (白玉京, 'the White-Jade Capital', the divine metropolis, vv. 28, 63) and Thiên-Đình (天庭, 'the Heavenly Court', v. 57)
entries.partOfSpeech: Caodai divine names, titles, and celestial toponyms (Sino-Vietnamese)
entries.literal: High-Tower; Jade-Emperor Supreme-Deity; Immortal-Elder; Most-High; Great-Merciful-Father; White-Jade-Capital; Heavenly-Court
entries.standardEnglish: usage varies between retaining all Sino-Vietnamese titles untranslated and rendering them; 'Cao Đài' is normally retained
entries.wohChoice: retain Cao Đài as an untranslated proper name; translate the descriptive titles and glosses in brackets on first use — Ngọc-Hoàng Thượng-Đế = 'the Jade Emperor, the Supreme Being'; Ngọc Đế = 'the Jade Emperor'; Tiên Ông = 'the Immortal Elder'; Đức Chí Tôn = 'the Most High'; Đại-Từ-Phụ = 'the Great Merciful Father'; Bạch-Ngọc-Kinh = 'the White-Jade Capital'; Thiên-Đình = 'the Heavenly Court'
entries.rationale: Cao Đài is the fixed proper name of the deity and the movement, and translating it ('the High Tower') would both estrange the reader and obscure that it functions as a name, so it is retained untranslated — the one term the whole tradition keeps — while the descriptive Sino-Vietnamese titles are rendered because each carries transparent lexical content a reader can and should see (the Jade-Emperor and Immortal-Elder titles locate the deity in the Daoist pantheon; Đại-Từ-Phụ imports the Buddhist 'Great Merciful Father'). The retain-vs-translate line is drawn to keep the surface text a defensible independent rendering rather than a transliteration wall, and to avoid importing the standard English Caodai glosses wholesale. The choice is inferred because the exact line (retain the name, gloss the titles) is a defensible editorial policy rather than the only possible one — a maximalist could retain every title. Named references: Đào Duy Anh, Hán-Việt Từ-điển, s.vv. 高臺, 玉皇, 至尊, 白玉京; Victor L. Oliver, Caodai Spiritism (Brill, 1976); Sergei Blagov, Caodaism (Nova Science, 2001).

entries.lemma: Tam-Kỳ Phổ-Độ (三期普度), the central Caodai doctrinal term: the third of three great salvific dispensations or 'openings' of the Way. Tam-Kỳ = 'the Third Period/Epoch'; Phổ = 普 'universal, spread everywhere, make manifest'; Độ = 度 'to ferry across, save, deliver' (the Buddhist pāramitā 'crossing over'). Occurs at vv. 55, 73, 75; the movement's full institutional name is Đại-Đạo Tam-Kỳ Phổ-Độ
entries.literal: 'the Third-Period Universal Ferrying-Across / Universal Deliverance' — i.e. the third universal salvation
entries.standardEnglish: English Caodai usage varies: 'Third Universal Salvation', 'Third Amnesty of God', 'Third Universal Redemption', 'Third Period of Universal Salvation'; the French-Caodai tradition fixes 'la Troisième Amnistie' ('the Third Amnesty')
entries.wohChoice: 'Third Universal Amnesty (Tam-Kỳ Phổ-Độ)' as the fixed project-standard NAME (matching this book's _meta subtitle and the site/catalog), with the literal sense 'universal deliverance / ferrying-across of all beings' carried in commentary; where the text ITSELF parses the components (v. 75: 'Phổ là bày ra … Độ … cứu chúng sanh'), the etymological exposition is preserved literally ('Phổ is to spread abroad … Độ is to save living beings') and the component word Phổ-độ is kept romanized there
entries.rationale: 'Amnesty' is the established project rendering (this book's _meta subtitle, the catalog, and the site) and it is not an ad hoc choice: the French-Caodai tradition, which is contemporaneous with and internal to the movement's own self-presentation, fixed the term as 'la Grande Amnistie' / 'la Troisième Amnistie de Dieu' — a general pardon granted to all souls in this third and final redemptive epoch — so 'Amnesty' renders the doctrinal sense (a universal remission) rather than the etymology. The literal core of Phổ-Độ is nonetheless 'universal deliverance / to ferry all beings across' (Phổ 普 'universal' + Độ 度 'to ferry across, save'), which the WoH translation preserves in commentary and, crucially, in the surface text at v. 75, where the séance dialogue itself glosses the two graphs and must not be overwritten by the fixed name. The choice is marked inferred, not direct, because 'Amnesty' is a doctrinally-motivated rendering that diverges from the plain lexical value, and it is explicitly flagged in the editor report for reviewer confirmation and project-wide standardization; the draft's 'Third Universal Salvation' is superseded. Named references: Gabriel Gobron, Histoire et philosophie du Caodaisme (Dervy, 1949) for 'Amnistie'; Đào Duy Anh, Hán-Việt Từ-điển s.vv. 普, 度; Janet Hoskins, The Divine Eye and the Diaspora (Hawai'i, 2015).

entries.source: cơ / thủ cơ / chấp bút / phò cơ / phò loan / giáng cơ / cơ bút
entries.translit: cơ / thủ cơ / chấp bút / phò cơ / phò loan / giáng cơ / cơ bút
entries.lemma: the spirit-writing (séance) apparatus: cơ (機/乩, the planchette / beaked basket, French corbeille-à-bec, the pointer that traces characters); thủ cơ (手乩, 'to hold/wield the planchette'); chấp bút (執筆, 'to hold the pen' — automatic writing); phò cơ (扶乩, 'to support/assist the planchette', the medium's office); phò loan (扶鸞, 'to support the phoenix', the paired-medium method — standard term, not lexicalized in ch. 1); giáng cơ (降乩, 'to descend onto the planchette', of a spirit); cơ bút (乩筆, the séance-writing craft in general)
entries.literal: planchette; hold-the-planchette; hold-the-pen; support-the-planchette; support-the-phoenix; descend-to-the-planchette; planchette-and-pen
entries.standardEnglish: no fixed English rendering; spiritualist calques ('automatic writing', 'psychography') or Chinese 'fuji / spirit-writing' are variously used
entries.wohChoice: descriptive English glosses with the Vietnamese term parenthesized on first use: cơ = 'the planchette (cơ)' / 'the spirit-writing planchette'; thủ cơ = 'to wield the planchette'; chấp bút = 'to hold the pen'; phò cơ = 'to support the planchette'; giáng cơ = 'to descend to the séance'; cơ bút / bút cơ = 'the work of pen and planchette'; phò loan reserved (not in ch. 1) as 'to support the phoenix [the paired-medium method]'
entries.rationale: The séance apparatus is the material means by which the entire text was produced and has no standard English equivalent, so the WoH translation renders each term by a transparent descriptive gloss with the Vietnamese parenthesized, rather than importing the Western-spiritualist calques ('automatic writing', 'psychography') that would falsely assimilate the Caodai cơ-bút to the séance-room of Anglo-American Spiritualism, or leaving the terms as an untranslated wall. The gloss 'planchette' for cơ is chosen with care: the cơ is specifically the corbeille-à-bec / beaked basket to which a writing stylus is fixed (the East-Asian fuji 扶乩 instrument), for which 'planchette' is the nearest English apparatus-word, and the commentary notes the mechanism. The choice is inferred because the descriptive-gloss policy is a defensible editorial line, not the only one (a maximalist could retain cơ / phò loan untranslated throughout). Named references: Đào Duy Anh, Hán-Việt Từ-điển s.vv. 乩, 扶鸞; Jérémy Jammes, Les Oracles du Cao Đài (Les Indes savantes, 2014), the standard study of Caodai spirit-writing; David A. Palmer & Vincent Goossaert on Chinese fuji spirit-writing.

entries.lemma: the Caodai spiritual-anthropology terms: Chơn-Thần (真神, 'True Spirit'), the perispirit / spiritual body, which the source itself glosses 'nhị xác thân (périsprit) … xác thân thiêng-liêng' = 'the second body (périsprit), the spiritual body' (v. 12); phách (魄, the vital/corporeal soul, the yin body-soul that anchors the person to the flesh, v. 9); chơn-linh (真靈, 'true numen/spirit', the higher spirit, v. 16); linh-hồn (靈魂, 'soul', v. 16); paired at v. 49/55 with Tinh-Khí-Thần (Essence-Breath-Spirit, the Three Treasures)
entries.standardEnglish: 'perispirit' (following the text's own French-Spiritist gloss), 'astral/spiritual body', or literal 'True Spirit'
entries.wohChoice: Chơn-Thần = 'the True Spirit (Chơn-Thần)' (literal 真神), with the source's own 'périsprit' gloss preserved at v. 12; phách = 'the vital-body (phách)'; chơn-linh = 'the true-spirit / True-Spirit'; linh-hồn = 'soul'
entries.rationale: Chơn-Thần is rendered by its literal lexical value 'True Spirit' (真 chơn 'true, real' + 神 thần 'spirit'), rather than adopting the text's parenthetical 'périsprit' as the primary English, because the graphic-etymological rendering keeps the term legible within the Sino-Vietnamese conceptual field it belongs to, while the périsprit gloss — Allan Kardec's Spiritist term for the semi-material envelope of the soul, which the séance circle knew from French Spiritism — is preserved exactly where the source itself supplies it (v. 12), documenting the historical borrowing without letting it govern the translation throughout. phách is distinguished as the corporeal/vital soul (the yin 魄 po of the classical hun-po 魂魄 pair) that 'holds back' the Chơn-Thần, which the reading 'vital-body' preserves. The choice is inferred because the literal-over-périsprit decision and the phách rendering are defensible readings rather than the single consensus. Named references: Allan Kardec, Le Livre des Esprits (1857), for périsprit; the hun-po soul-dualism in Đào Duy Anh, Hán-Việt Từ-điển s.vv. 魂, 魄; Victor L. Oliver, Caodai Spiritism (Brill, 1976).

entries.lemma: the four-tier ascending celestial hierarchy of attained beings: Thần (神, 'Spirit(s)/Deity', the lowest divine rank), Thánh (聖, 'Saint/Sage'), Tiên (仙, 'Immortal/transcendent'), Phật (佛, 'Buddha', the highest) — with Nhơn (人, 'Humanity') as the base rank, together giving the five Ngũ chi Đại-Đạo (Five Branches of the Great Way, vv. 106-107). Recurs at vv. 13, 49, 50, 57, 72-73, 107
entries.standardEnglish: Thần = 'Spirit(s) / Genie / Deity / Angel'; Thánh = 'Saint / Sage'; Tiên = 'Immortal / Genie / Fairy'; Phật = 'Buddha'; the older French-Caodai apparatus calques Thần (and sometimes Tiên) as 'génie'
entries.wohChoice: the ascending set fixed as Spirits – Saints – Immortals – Buddhas; and for the Ngũ chi Đại-Đạo (v. 107): the Way of Humanity (Nhơn-đạo) / of the Spirits (Thần-đạo) / of the Saints (Thánh-đạo) / of the Immortals (Tiên-đạo) / of the Buddhas (Phật-đạo)
entries.rationale: The four ranks form a deliberate graded hierarchy that the text repeatedly counts on (the prostration doctrine of vv. 49-52 assigns three bows to Thần/Thánh, nine to Tiên/Phật, twelve to God), so the English must fix one distinct term per rank and preserve the ascending order rather than blur them. 'Spirits – Saints – Immortals – Buddhas' is chosen because it renders each graph by its nearest settled English equivalent while keeping the ladder legible: Thần 神 as 'Spirits' (the generic divine/tutelary rank) over the French-Caodai calque 'génie' (which mistranslates to English readers as a lamp-genie) and over 'Angels' (which imports an Abrahamic frame the Sino field does not carry); Tiên 仙 as 'Immortals' (the Daoist transcendents) over 'Genii/Fairies'; Thánh and Phật by their standard 'Saints' and 'Buddhas'. The choice is inferred because the label-set is a defensible mapping rather than the only one, and the 'génie'/'Angels' alternatives are recorded for the reviewer. Named references: Đào Duy Anh, Hán-Việt Từ-điển s.vv. 神, 聖, 仙, 佛; Gabriel Gobron, Histoire et philosophie du Caodaisme (1949) for the 'génie' calque; Sergei Blagov, Caodaism (2001) on the five-tier Ngũ chi.

entries.source: Giáo-Tông / Đầu-Sư / Hộ-Pháp / Giáo-Hữu / Thiên-Phong / Thiên-Phục
entries.translit: Giáo-Tông / Đầu-Sư / Hộ-Pháp / Giáo-Hữu / Thiên-Phong / Thiên-Phục
entries.lemma: the Caodai sacerdotal offices and their investiture: Giáo-Tông (教宗, the supreme leader of the Cửu Trùng Đài / Nine-Sphere Executive Palace, conventionally 'Pope', glossed at v. 111 'anh cả' = 'eldest brother'); Đầu-Sư (頭師, lit. 'Head-Master', conventionally 'Cardinal'); Hộ-Pháp (護法, 'Dharma-Protector / Defender of the Law', head of the Hiệp Thiên Đài / Heaven-Union Legislative Palace); Giáo-Hữu (教友, lit. 'religion-friend', conventionally 'Priest'); Thiên-Phong (天封, 'Heavenly Ordination', vv. 80, 82); Thiên-Phục (天服, 'Heavenly Vestment', v. 83); the three branch-colors Thái (Buddhist, yellow) / Thượng (Daoist, blue) / Ngọc (Confucian, red), v. 83
entries.partOfSpeech: Caodai ecclesiastical titles and investiture terms (Sino-Vietnamese)
entries.literal: Religion-Ancestor/Pope; Head-Master/Cardinal; Dharma-Protector; religion-friend/Priest; Heaven-Sealing/Ordination; Heaven-Vestment
entries.standardEnglish: conventional Catholic-analogy English: Giáo-Tông = 'Pope', Đầu-Sư = 'Cardinal', Giáo-Hữu = 'Priest', Hộ-Pháp = 'Dharma-Protector'
entries.wohChoice: retain the Vietnamese titles with a bracketed conventional gloss on first use: 'the Giáo-Tông [Pope]', 'the three Đầu-Sư [Cardinals]', 'the Hộ-Pháp [the Defender of the Dharma]', 'Giáo-Hữu [Priest]'; Thiên-Phong = 'Heavenly Ordination'; Thiên-Phục = 'Heavenly Vestment'. The v. 111 crux ('Đầu-Sư … nghĩa là Giáo-Hữu') is rendered by the literal sense of Giáo-Hữu, 'religious brethren', with the crux flagged (see collation entry)
entries.rationale: The Caodai hierarchy was consciously built on a Roman-Catholic organizational template (Pope, Cardinals, a college of dignitaries) fused with Buddhist-Daoist titulature, so the conventional Catholic-analogy English is genuinely informative and is retained as a bracketed gloss — but the Vietnamese title is kept as the primary term because the offices are not identical to their Catholic namesakes and because the three governing Đài (Bát Quái / Cửu Trùng / Hiệp Thiên) have no Western equivalent at all. The v. 111 gloss 'ba phẩm Đầu-Sư, nghĩa là Giáo-Hữu' is a genuine crux: read with Giáo-Hữu as the technical rank 'Priest' it is doctrinally anomalous (a Đầu-Sư outranks a Priest), so the WoH translation reads Giáo-Hữu here in its transparent literal sense 教友 'religion-friends / religious brethren' (the senior brethren of the fellowship), parallel to the immediately preceding gloss of Giáo-Tông as 'anh cả' (eldest brother), and flags the crux for the second witness. The choice is inferred because the retain-plus-gloss policy and the Giáo-Hữu reading are defensible editorial judgements, not the only possible ones. Named references: Đào Duy Anh, Hán-Việt Từ-điển s.vv. 教宗, 護法, 教友; Jayne S. Werner, Peasant Politics and Religious Sectarianism (Yale SEA, 1981) on Caodai organization; Sergei Blagov, Caodaism (2001).

entries.source: Càn-Khôn / Âm-Dương / Tinh-Khí-Thần / Tam Bửu / Càn – Khôn
entries.translit: Càn-Khôn / Âm-Dương / Tinh-Khí-Thần / Tam Bửu / Càn – Khôn
entries.lemma: the cosmological field: Càn-Khôn (乾坤, the trigrams ☰ Qián 'Heaven' and ☷ Kūn 'Earth', a merism for the whole cosmos/universe; vv. 15, 21, 46, 52 Càn-Khôn Thế-Giái 'the Cosmos and the World', 109); Âm-Dương (陰陽, Yin and Yang; vv. 46, 48); Tinh-Khí-Thần (精氣神, Essence-Breath-Spirit, the internal-alchemy triad; v. 49); Tam Bửu (三寶, the 'Three Treasures' = Tinh-Khí-Thần; v. 55); the two trigrams named singly Càn / Khôn (v. 108, 'Càn vô đắc khán, Khôn vô đắc duyệt')
entries.literal: Qian-Kun (Heaven-and-Earth); Yin-Yang; Essence-Breath-Spirit; Three Treasures; the Qian / Kun trigrams
entries.standardEnglish: Càn-Khôn variously 'Heaven and Earth' (preserving the trigram merism) or 'the Cosmos/Universe'; Tinh-Khí-Thần often left as 'jing-qi-shen'
entries.wohChoice: Càn-Khôn = 'the Cosmos (Càn-Khôn)'; Càn-Khôn Thế-Giái = 'the Cosmos and the World'; Âm-Dương = 'Yin and Yang'; Tinh-Khí-Thần = 'Essence, Breath, and Spirit'; Tam Bửu = 'the Three Treasures'; the single trigrams Càn / Khôn rendered 'Heaven … Earth' with the trigram sense noted (v. 108)
entries.rationale: Càn-Khôn is the two-trigram merism 乾坤 (Qián ☰ + Kūn ☷) that classical Chinese cosmology uses as a totality-figure for the created universe, and the WoH translation renders it 'the Cosmos' (with the Vietnamese retained) where it functions as that totality — vv. 15, 21, 52 — because 'Heaven and Earth' there would read as a mere pair rather than the whole, while at v. 108, where the two trigrams are named singly and separately ('Càn vô đắc khán, Khôn vô đắc duyệt', Heaven could not be seen, Earth could not be surveyed), the merism is unpacked to 'Heaven … Earth' and the trigram basis is noted. Tinh-Khí-Thần is rendered by the settled internal-alchemy English 'Essence, Breath, and Spirit' and identified with the Tam Bửu 'Three Treasures', preserving the doctrine of v. 55 (that this Amnesty restores Thần to Tinh-Khí to complete the triad). The choice is inferred because the context-sensitive Càn-Khôn split ('Cosmos' vs 'Heaven … Earth') and the alchemical-triad English are defensible readings rather than the sole option. Named references: the Yijing trigram values in Đào Duy Anh, Hán-Việt Từ-điển s.vv. 乾, 坤; the jing-qi-shen triad in the Daoist internal-alchemy literature (Isabelle Robinet, Taoist Meditation); Victor L. Oliver, Caodai Spiritism (1976).

entries.source: Đạo / Đại-Đạo / Chánh-Giáo / Thánh-Giáo / Phàm-Giáo / Đạo-Đức / Chánh-Thể
entries.translit: Đạo / Đại-Đạo / Chánh-Giáo / Thánh-Giáo / Phàm-Giáo / Đạo-Đức / Chánh-Thể
entries.lemma: the Way-and-religion field: Đạo (道, 'the Way' — both the metaphysical Dao and, by extension, the Caodai religion, e.g. 'Đạo phát trễ', 'danh Đạo', 'áo Đạo'); Đại-Đạo (大道, 'the Great Way'); the -Giáo (教 'teaching/religion') compounds Chánh-Giáo (正教, 'True Religion'), Thánh-Giáo (聖教, 'Holy Teaching'), Phàm-Giáo (凡教, 'Worldly Religion'); Đạo-Đức (道德, 'Virtue / the Way and its Power', vv. 20, 29); Chánh-Thể (政體, 'Governing Body / polity', v. 110)
entries.literal: the Way; the Great Way; True-Teaching; Holy-Teaching; Common-Teaching; Way-Virtue; Governing-Body
entries.standardEnglish: Đạo variously 'the Way', 'the Tao', or contextually 'the religion/the Faith'
entries.wohChoice: Đạo = 'the Way' UNIFORMLY (a single gloss even where the referent is the Caodai religion), with the religious sense carried by context; Đại-Đạo = 'the Great Way'; Chánh-Giáo = 'the True Religion'; Thánh-Giáo = 'the Holy Teaching'; Phàm-Giáo = 'Worldly Religion'; Đạo-Đức = 'Virtue'; Chánh-Thể = 'a Governing Body'
entries.rationale: Đạo carries both 'the Way' (the metaphysical Dao) and 'the religion' (the Caodai faith) within a single word, and the WoH translation keeps the uniform gloss 'the Way' rather than alternating with 'the religion' because the ambiguity is deliberate and load-bearing in the source — the whole Caodai claim is that the institution IS the Way, so splitting the English into two words would resolve a fusion the text wants held together, and the religious referent is recoverable from context in every case. The -Giáo compounds, by contrast, lexicalize 'teaching/religion' explicitly (教) and are rendered with 'Religion/Teaching' to mark the contrast the text draws at vv. 108-109 between the Holy Teaching (Thánh-Giáo) and its degeneration into a merely Worldly Religion (Phàm-Giáo). The choice is inferred because uniform-'Way' is a defensible policy rather than the only one (contextual alternation is legitimate and is recorded as the alternative). Named references: the semantic range of 道 in Đào Duy Anh, Hán-Việt Từ-điển s.v. 道; the Dao/religion doubling discussed in Janet Hoskins, The Divine Eye and the Diaspora (2015).

entries.lemma: lạy, the full ritual prostration (kneeling and touching the forehead to the ground), and its doctrinally-fixed counts, expounded in the catechism of vv. 45-52: two lạy for the living; four for the departed mortal (two for the human portion + one Heaven + one Earth); three for Spirits and Saints (the third rank of Heaven; also Tinh-Khí-Thần united); nine for Immortals and Buddhas (the nine Powers of the Nine Heavens, Cửu-Thiên); twelve for God (the Thập nhị Khai-Thiên, the Twelve who Opened Heaven; twelve = God's own number)
entries.wohChoice: 'prostration' throughout (not 'bow', which understates the full kneeling act, nor 'kowtow', which carries pejorative English connotations); the counts rendered as cardinals with the doctrinal rationale preserved verbatim from the catechism
entries.rationale: lạy is the full prostration — kneeling and bringing the forehead to the ground — not a standing bow, so 'prostration' is chosen over 'bow' (which an English reader hears as a mere inclination and which would break the numerological doctrine that grades reverence by bodily repetition) and over 'kowtow' (accurate in gesture but freighted with pejorative colonial-English connotation). Consistency matters because the counts are doctrinally exact and mutually contrastive across vv. 45-52 — two/three/four/nine/twelve encode a whole cosmology of rank (human, Spirit/Saint, Immortal/Buddha, God) — so a single fixed English term is required for the arithmetic to read. The choice is inferred because 'prostration' vs 'bow' is a defensible register decision rather than the only possible rendering. Named references: Đào Duy Anh, Hán-Việt Từ-điển s.v. 拜 (bái); the ritual-numerology of the Caodai prostrations in Victor L. Oliver, Caodai Spiritism (Brill, 1976) and the Tòa Thánh Tây Ninh liturgical manuals.

entries.source: Nhiên-Đăng Cổ-Phật / Thích-Ca Mâu-Ni / Như-Lai / Thái-Thượng / Ngươn-Thỉ / Nam-mô / A-Tỳ / Bồng Đảo / Lý-Bạch / tam đồ / Thiên Tôn
entries.translit: Nhiên-Đăng Cổ-Phật / Thích-Ca Mâu-Ni / Như-Lai / Thái-Thượng / Ngươn-Thỉ / Nam-mô / A-Tỳ / Bồng Đảo / Lý-Bạch / tam đồ / Thiên Tôn
entries.lemma: the Sino-Vietnamese proper-name and Buddhist-loan field, rendered by standard Sanskrit/Chinese equivalents: Nhiên-Đăng Cổ-Phật (燃燈古佛) = Dīpaṃkara, the Ancient Buddha; Thích-Ca Mâu-Ni / Mậu-Ni (釋迦牟尼) = Śākyamuni; Như-Lai (如來) = Tathāgata; Thái-Thượng (太上, i.e. Thái-Thượng Lão-Quân 太上老君) = Taishang Laojun, the deified Laozi; Ngươn-Thỉ (元始, i.e. Nguyên-Thủy Thiên-Tôn 元始天尊) = Yuanshi Tianzun, the Primordial-Beginning Heavenly-Venerable; Nam-mô (南無) = Sanskrit namaḥ, 'homage to'; A-Tỳ (阿鼻) = Avīci, the deepest hell; Bồng Đảo (蓬島, Bồng-Lai) = Penglai, the Isle of the Immortals; Lý-Bạch (李白) = Li Bai, the Tang poet (here the invisible Giáo-Tông); tam đồ (三途) = the Three Evil Paths/destinies; Thiên Tôn (天尊) = 'Heavenly Venerable' (v. 85, Cửu Thiên Cảm Ứng Lôi Thinh Phổ Hoá Thiên Tôn)
entries.literal: Lamp-Lighting Ancient-Buddha; Śākyamuni; Thus-Come-One; Supreme-Highest; Primordial-Beginning; homage-to; Avīci; Penglai-Isle; Li Bai; Three-Paths; Heavenly-Venerable
entries.standardEnglish: these theonyms are variously left transliterated in the Vietnamese or given Sanskrit/Chinese standard forms
entries.wohChoice: give the standard Sanskrit/Chinese identification with the Sino-Vietnamese retained in brackets: Nhiên-Đăng = Dīpaṃkara; Thích-Ca Mâu-Ni = Śākyamuni; Như-Lai = Tathāgata; Thái-Thượng = Taishang (Laojun); Ngươn-Thỉ = Yuanshi (Tianzun); Nam-mô = 'Homage'; A-Tỳ = Avīci; Bồng Đảo = 'the Isle of the Immortals (Penglai)'; Lý-Bạch = Li Bai; tam đồ = 'the Three Evil Paths'; Thiên Tôn = 'Heavenly Venerable'
entries.rationale: These are securely identified proper names and standard Buddhist/Daoist technical loans whose Sanskrit and Chinese forms are uncontested, so rendering them by their established equivalents (Dīpaṃkara, Śākyamuni, Tathāgata, Taishang Laojun, Yuanshi Tianzun, Avīci, Penglai) is a direct lexical fact, not an interpretive reading — the only editorial choice is to retain the Sino-Vietnamese in brackets so the reader can trace the identification. One point is flagged in commentary rather than resolved on the surface: the compressed 'Thái-Thượng Ngươn-Thỉ' of v. 69 names TWO distinct Daoist supreme deities (Taishang Laojun AND Yuanshi Tianzun), not a single figure, and the identity-formula ('… thị ngã … Kim viết Cao-Đài') collapses the founders of the Three Teachings into the one God now called Cao Đài. The Sino-Vietnamese spelling variation Mâu-Ni (v. 69) / Mậu-Ni (vv. 71-72) is a witness inconsistency for the same name Śākyamuni (see collation entry). Named references: the standard Sanskrit-Chinese-Vietnamese Buddhist onomastics in the Digital Dictionary of Buddhism (Charles Muller, ed.); Đào Duy Anh, Hán-Việt Từ-điển s.vv. 燃燈, 釋迦, 如來, 太上, 元始, 阿鼻, 蓬萊; the Penglai/Bồng-Lai immortal-isle motif in Daoist geography.

entries.translit: [single daotam.info witness; six+ witness cruxes retained in vi, intended reading in en]
entries.lemma: the collation framework for the TNHT-WoH source: a SINGLE working witness — the daotam.info e-text (mirror of the Sydney Centre for Studies in Caodaism transcription), collated 2026-07-02 (93/111 verses machine-matched NFC-normalized; the ~18 unmatched are the recurring signature header and short liturgical lines, differing only in punctuation/line-breaking). A second printed Tòa Thánh Tây Ninh witness is DESIRABLE before sign-off and is pending. Retained witness cruxes (vi kept verbatim; en renders the evident intended reading): (a) v. 32 'Thiên-Điêu' for 'Thiên-Điều' 天條 (the Heavenly Law); (b) v. 40 'Đ I-BỒ-TÁT' for 'ĐẠI-BỒ-TÁT'; (c) v. 26 'tứ [riêng]' most likely for 'ý [riêng]' (private mind); (d) v. 40 'mỗi gặt' obscure, read 'each [prostration/time]'; (e) v. 69 'Mâu-Ni' vs vv. 71-72 'Mậu-Ni' (Śākyamuni), inconsistent; (f) v. 92 'Xữ' for 'Xử' 杵 (the Giáng-Ma-Xử, Demon-Quelling Pestle); plus (g) v. 98 'Vi-Hộ Pháp' most likely for 'vị Hộ-Pháp' (the Hộ-Pháp); (h) v. 111 'Đầu-Sư … nghĩa là Giáo-Hữu' semantic crux (see sacerdotal entry)
entries.literal: the single-witness collation framework and its retained cruxes
entries.wohChoice: the daotam.info witness retained as the working source; all cruxes kept verbatim in the vi field and rendered by their evident intended reading in en, each recorded here and in per-verse commentary; a second Tòa Thánh Tây Ninh printed witness flagged as pending before final sign-off; the legacy U+00D0 (Ð ETH) normalized to U+0110 (Đ) with no other character changes
entries.rationale: Unlike the Hidden-Words source (two witnesses, OL vs BWC), TNHT Volume One is here collated against a SINGLE electronic witness (daotam.info), so this entry documents that limitation and records every point where the witness is corrupt or internally inconsistent, keeping the English auditable: the vi field preserves the witness verbatim (including the ETH→Đ normalization, which is a pure encoding fix, not a textual change), while the en field renders the evidently intended reading and flags the emendation rather than silently correcting it. The eight recorded cruxes are all benign and non-doctrinal — orthographic slips (Thiên-Điêu/Thiên-Điều, Đ I/ĐẠI, Xữ/Xử), a probable homophone error (tứ/ý), an obscure form (mỗi gặt), a name-spelling inconsistency (Mâu/Mậu-Ni), a probable word-boundary error (Vi/vị Hộ-Pháp), and one genuine semantic crux (Giáo-Hữu at v. 111) — none of which changes the sense, but all of which must be checked against a printed Tòa Thánh Tây Ninh edition before the translation is signed off as verified. This is claim_type direct: it records collation facts and editorial emendations, not interpretive readings. Named references: the daotam.info e-text and the Sydney Centre for Studies in Caodaism transcription (collationWitnesses in source-vi-1.json); project policy strategy-library-acquisition.md, requiring a second witness before final sign-off.
